title: Mary's Room
summary:
Frank Jackson imagined Mary, a brilliant scientist who has spent her whole life in a black-and-white room, learning about the world through black-and-white books and a black-and-white television. She becomes the world's expert on colour vision: she knows every physical fact about what goes on when we see ripe tomatoes, or the sky. Then she is let out, and sees red for the first time. Does she learn something new? Jackson argued in 1982 that she does, and so the physical facts are not all the facts: what it is like to see red is left out.

Critics replied that she gains only a new ability, to imagine and recognise red (David Lewis, Laurence Nemirow); or a new way of knowing a fact she already knew; or that if she really knew everything physical she would not be surprised at all (Daniel Dennett, who has her captors try to trick her with a blue banana). Jackson himself later changed his mind, and came to think physicalism was true after all.
citations: Frank Jackson, "What Mary Didn't Know," Journal of Philosophy 83(5) (1986): 291–295
David Lewis, "What Experience Teaches," Proceedings of the Russellian Society 13 (1988): 29–57
Martine Nida-Rümelin and Donnchadh O Conaill, "Qualia: The Knowledge Argument," Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qualia-knowledge/
